caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 693 of 1968
lawyer:
M. S. M. Nasirul Islam—For the Appellant 
M. A. Rahim—For the Respondent.
parties:
Jaha Baksha Par ------ Appellant.
Vs.
Fazle Karim Biswas & ors------ Respondent
full_judgment:
2. Facts leading to this appeal in short are that the land described in the schedule to the plaint belonged to the plaintiffs Fazle Karim Biswas and Nasim Biswas. They took loan of Tk. 200/00 from the defendant Jaha Baksha, a village money lender and as security of the loan mortgaged the suit land with him as a token of that mortgage he obtained a patta from the plaintiff dated 9.3.53 (Ext. A), according to the local custorn on an oral agreement that the defendant will reconvey the land when the plaintiff would pay back the loan. It was further stipulated in that agreement that the land will remain with the plaintiff (lessor) and half of the produce of the suit land would be paid to the defendant (lessee) by way of interest of the loan till the loan is repaid. The plaintiff possessed the land paid half of the barga crops as per term of the agreement to the defendant for quite a number of years till 1953.  Thereafter the property was put to auction by the landlord for arrears of rent due from the plaintiff as tenant. The plaintiff filed a Misc. Case being Misc. Case No. 344/45 and got the sale set aside and since then the plaintiff continued to remain in possession all these years and continued to pay half the produce of the suit land as per the oral agreement but the defendant in violation of the agreement for re-conveyance, in spite of plaintiff's demand for the same after tendering the loan money, forcibly entered into the disputed land end dispossessed the plaintiff on 12.3.58. Hence the suit for Specific Performance of Contract and recovery of khas possession. 

 3. The defendant contested the suit by filing a written statement contending inter alia that the plaintiff never mortgaged the suit land but it was leased out to the defendant by plaintiff on payment of selami of Tk. 200/00 by means of a patta in the year 1953 and since then the defendants are in possession of the property. Further case of the defendant is that there was no oral agreement for re-conveyance of the suit land but the defendant bad always paid root to the plaintiff as a subtenant and obtained dakhila from the plaintiff and also got his name recorded as such in the Revisional Re-cord of Rights. So the plaintiff has no cause of action and the suit is liable to be dismissed. On these pleadings the panics brought out the suit. 

 4. The court of first instance upon a. consideration of the pleadings of the parties and the evidence on record, decreed the suit on a finding that the patta was in fact a mortgage deed and not a lease document, proved by. subsequent conduct of the parties and also by oral agreement as to that, and also having it proved by independent witnesses and in that view of the matter the court found right, title and interest of the plaintiff. The plaintiff had to deposit 200/00 taka within 15 days and then to execute and register a deed of reconveyance in favour of the plaintiff within 1 month and in default the plaintiff would be entitled to execute and register it through the Court. On appeal the said was affirmed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Additional Court, Jessore by his judgment of 28th October, 1967. As against that this appeal has been preferred before this Court and thereafter vide Civil Rule No. 656(9/69 dated 1.5.69 the proceeding of Title Execution Case No. 7/69 of the 3rd Court of Munsif, Jessore, was stayed. 

 5. Mr. Nasirul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal having taken me through the judgment of the courts below and the evidence on record, has urged that the courts below erred in law in not considering that the dakhila Ext. B which clearly shows payment of rent by defendant to the plaintiff himself, would contradict the plaintiff's claim of mortgaging the property with the defendant but in spite of that the courts below came to an erroneous finding of fact to the effect that the suit property was mortgaged. It was thus bad in law. He has further urged that the patta Ext. A  clearly shows that the transaction was a lease end not a mortgage but inspite of that the court ill violation of the provisions of section 92 of the Evidence Act had admitted the oral evidence to vary the terms of the said instrument. Hence, the finding of fact that the document Ext. A was not a. lease document but mortgage was arrived at by taking a wrong view of the law and in violation of section 92 of the Evidence Act and therefore, the said need to be set aside.  Mr. Nasirul Islam has further urged that the courts below was not competent to entertain the suit view of the fact that the defendant appellants were admittedly in possession for long years after the patta in 1953 and therefore, the suit instituted in 1965 was long after 12 years and therefore, was not maintainable being barred under the Limitation Act. He has further urged that the courts were competent to giver relief to the parties even if no issues were framed on a particular point if there were evidence on record on either way, causing no prejudice for the parties. But the courts below did not take into consideration this aspect of the case. This being a point of law can be raised even at the time of appeal. He has further urged that the courts below failed to take into consideration the point that the defendant appellant was also a petitioner in the sale not aside case and yet came to an erroneous findings of facts as to the absence of the appellant in that proceeding and all these having prompted the court to come to a finding that the tenancy interest still existed in favour of the plaintiff and it having arrived at by a non-consideration of the evidence on record, need to be set aside. 

 6. Mr. M.A. Rahim, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff respondents on the other hand has contended that the findings of fact of both the courts below as to the existence of the oral agreement contemporaneous to the patta in 1953 by which the parties agreed the suit land to be on usufructuary mortgage on receipt of 200/00 taka from the mortgagee as consideration, and the possession having remained with the mortgagor with the right of reconveyance after payment of rent, the said finding of fact having been arrived at after full consideration of the evidence on record and the patta deed, they said could not be said to be a finding of fact arrived at by causing an error of law or of procedure which could be set aside by this Court. Mr. Rahim has further urged that in the presence of an oral agreemenlas to usufructuary mortgage and subsequent reconveyance, the patta itself would not establish the real intention of the parties and that being so the oral agreement would be admissible under section 92 of the Evidence Act in order to find out from the surrounding circumstances the real intention of the parties to the contract and the nature and purpose of the contract. It would not be a case to vary the terms as such but a case of misrepresentation as contemplated under Proviso 1and 6 to Section 92 of the Evidence Act. Hence, it is contended by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the courts below did not act illegally in admitting the oral evidence in any violation of the Provisions of Section 92 of the Evidence Act as contended. 

 7. In the instant case, there are facts which are not disputed by either of the party namely that the original tenancy belonged to the plaintiff's predecessor Janab Ali Biswas and that he took Taka 200/00 from defendant Jaha Baksha Par and thereafter the patta was executed (Ext. A) which was of the year 1953 and that it clearly showed the creation of a lease of the tenanted land by Janab Ali Biswas, the loanee in favour of loaner Jaha Baksha Par. According to plaintiff respondent Taka 200/00 was obtained as loan only and not as salami and that though Ext. A, the patta recites a lease in favour of defendant executed in the year 1953 by the plaintiff's predecessor Janab Ali Biswas, the transaction indeed was an usufructuary mortgage with a conditional reconveyance and not a lease though the plaintiff's predecessor had received rent from the defendant by granting dakhila and though defendant's name was recorded in the Revisional Record of Right as a tenant. The defendant-appellant on the other hand contended that there was no oral agreement. There was only one agreement and that was the patta duly registered and nothing more and nothing less. Further, that this registered patta was acted upon by the plaintiff's predecessors by accepting rents from the defendants by granting dakhila and it was further acted upon by the inclusion of the defendant-appellants name as tenant in the relevant S.A. Khatian and hence the terms of the document granting lease cannot be varied by oral evidence. 

 8. Under the law oral evidence to modify or vary or alter the "terms" of a written document would not be admissible in evidence under the provisions of Section 92 of the Evidence Act. As to this legal embargo there is no dispute. What was agitated was whether Ext. A being a patta comes within the provision of section 92 of the Evidence Act which speaks of a bilateral document, any grant or disposition of property or any matter required by law to be reduced in form of a document. A patta is to be written in the form of a document and after acceptance by the tenant it become a bilateral document creating interest, an instrument disposing property and if registered, as in this case would come within the object as contained in section 92, of the Evidence Act and admissible in evidence. 

 17. This is an appeal from a decree of affirmance. It had been found by both the courts below on evidence on record that the defendant was a money lender and he was in the habit of securing his loan by obtaining patta or document of lease from the borrower and in the instant case it was a mere loan on agreement for reconveyance of the land on refund of the loan. In support of this the court referred to a number of other documents submitted by the plaintiff being Ext. 1-to 1(c) which showed as to how and why the very defendant money lender had obtained those case documents from various other borrowers by advancing ken as a security and when they had refunded the loan, the patta was returned back, with his endorsement on the back of those documents which endorsements were admitted by the defendant money lender explaining that those were refunded by him out of pity. On a reference to the evidence on record as deposed by the executants of those other pattas, subsequently returned by the defendant money lender, it is seen that all of them supported the plaintiffs case that the defendant was a money lender and he always advanced loan by obtaining patta and it is known to all borrowers at the time they executed the patta in the form of a lease and thus they would know that the said lease would be a mere paper transaction. P.W. 2 and P.W. 3 stated that they were present when the plaintiff executed the document of patta and that at the time of execution it was agreed that the patta would be mere security for the money advanced and the land will be returned after the loan would be repaid. Further, it is seen that this so-called leased out property was put in auction for arrears of revenue and it was the plaintiff who alone filed the Miso. case for setting aside the sale which would not be the case if he had already ceased to be the tenant vide the alleged patta. The plaintiff accepted Dakhilas from Defendants and allowed his name to be recorded in settlement records but both the court found that it was done because the plaintiff was in good terms with the defendant and plaintiff being in possession had no threat to his actual Title. All these were arrived at by both the courts below with cogent reasons. 

 18. The contention that the courts below admitted evidence to vary the terms of the Patta in violation of the provisions contained in Section 92 of the Evidence Act and that the findings arrived at was erroneous has thus no basis. This appeal which has no substance, thus, needs to be dismissed. In the result, this appeal is dismissed. The judgment and decree appealed against are affirmed without any order as to cost in the facts and circumstances of the case. Send down the records at once.
